newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea makes goodwill moves ahead of defector talks.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea makes goodwill moves ahead of defector talks.

text.p: South Korea made fresh goodwill gestures towards rival North Korea on Tuesday on the eve of talks with China over the fate of a top-level Pyongyang defector holed up in Seoul's Beijing mission.
Seoul officials said the first South Koreans to visit the North since a submarine incursion froze contacts between the two countries last September arrived on Tuesday.
Separately, 26 officials from state-run Korea Electric Power Corp were due to visit North Korea on Saturday to prepare for construction of nuclear power plants, they said.
"We are trying to return inter-Korean relations to the level before the submarine incident," South Korean foreign ministry spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung told Reuters.
All contacts were frozen after a North Korean submarine dropped 26 intruders on a Southern beach last September.

Pyongyang issued a rare apology in December over the incident, prompting new progress in efforts to defuse tensions on the Korean peninsula. But the defection on February 12 of the North's top ideologue Hwang Jang-yop imposed new strains.
However, a unification ministry official in Seoul said the two Koreas had made cautious steps that could help promote a thaw in relations.

The ministry said Park Choon, managing director of Daewoo Corp, and three Daewoo technicians arrived in North Korea to resume business activities at the Northern port of Nampo where the Southern industrial giant has a joint venture.
"We believe the situation has improved somewhat and Daewoo can resume normal business activities," the official said.
Daewoo is the only South Korean company authorised to run a venture in the North. The plant makes clothes and bags.
Pyongyang announced last Friday that it would attend a briefing in New York on March 5 on peace talks proposed by the United States and South Korea, which would also include China.
The concession followed promises by Washington and Seoul to send $10 million and $6 million respectively in food aid to the failing Stalinist state.
Foreign ministry spokesman Lee said North Korea's sincerity could be gauged by the outcome of Seoul's negotiations with China to try to secure Hwang's passage to South Korea.
The defection request by Hwang, ranked 24 in Pyongyang's hierarchy, left China torn between a long-time ideological ally and a new business partner.
Lee said the pace of progress in the talks depended on Pyongyang's willingness to compromise.
Talks on Hwang, put on hold after the death of Chinese paramount leader Deng Xiaoping last week, were due to resume after Tuesday's funeral.
"We will ask Beijing to send Hwang to South Korea. Our talks with China will be a good indication of North Korea's sincerity towards us," Lee said.

Pyongyang initially accused Southern officials of kidnapping Hwang and demanded that China return him, but later appeared to backtrack, saying if Hwang had defected he would be stripped of his official rank.
Lee said North Korea's main goal was better ties with Washington.
"North Korea wants an easing of U.S. sanctions because of grave economic hardships. But its overtures to the U.S. do not necessarily mean that Pyongyang wants better ties with South Korea," he added.
Pyongyang remains technically at war with South Korea nearly half a century after their 1950-53 conflict ended in a truce.
